knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 70-year-old female visited the glaucoma clinic for a follow-up on her glaucoma status. She had a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia, both managed with oral medications. Her ophthalmic history included a diagnosis of normal tension glaucoma 10 years prior, for which she was using dorzolamide twice daily and tafluprost once daily in both eyes. Physical examination showed symmetrical ptosis and facial atrophy. She reported a family history of eye movement issues affecting her father, brother, daughter, and herself from a young age. The patient declined genetic testing, but a family pedigree was established. Her best corrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye. Pupillary reflexes and Ishihara color test results were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral cataracts, more pronounced in the right eye. Fundus examination showed minor pigmentary changes in both maculae. The optic discs had normal margins with peripapillary atrophy, and the cup/disc ratio was 0.7 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 10 mmHg in both eyes. Ocular motility examination indicated severe restriction in all directions

knowledge_fragments.content: While HSP primarily affects the lower limbs and progresses over time, CP typically presents as quadriplegia and is non-progressive. However, the distinction is often not clear-cut in clinical practice, especially when CP symptoms predominantly affect the lower limbs or when the onset of HSP is very early. Additionally, distinguishing progressive from non-progressive neuromotor abnormalities in CP is considered crucial for the genetic differential diagnosis of CP but remains challenging. This complexity arises because disease progression can be slow and sometimes only becomes evident later in life. In some cases, patients exhibit very early onset or severe symptoms from birth, making it hard to determine the clinical progression, as in Case 6. Furthermore, progression does not always impact motor function, but can manifest in other symptoms, such as worsening seizures, loss of vision or speech, or cognitive decline. The clinical diversity of each genetic disorder further complicates this issue, as progression varies significantly among individuals, from early onset to late onset. It is important to consider the child's underlying genetic diagnosis as well as to accurately describe their functional symptoms. This results in some children having two diagnoses – one of their HDCT and another describing functional complications. As the field of genetics moves forward we will be able to more accurately diagnose the genetic disorder underlying an individual child's hypermobility and the relevance of subtle phenotypic features in the mild HDCT will become clearer.

knowledge_fragments.content: Bone grafting is inevitably accompanied by connective tissue proliferation, either physiologically occurring in the healing process or as a foreign body reaction. Due to the wide variety of terms and lack of clear definitions, we derived the term “non-bone tissue” and included all corresponding parameters in this category. Synonyms were also grouped together in the subdivisions (e.g., marrow space and medullary space, connective tissue and stromal tissue, etc.). This was necessary because terms were phrased differently but had similar meanings. As can be seen from the results, soft tissue, connective tissue, bone marrow and non-mineralized tissue are the most frequently used. Bone marrow and marrow spaces are found in the trabecular spaces of spongy bone, hence the establishment of these parameters. The term “non-mineralized” tissue has been used by several authors but is unclear what it refers to—osteoid, connective tissue or other. Embryonically, blood vessels are also made of connective tissue, but due to their rare occurrence in studies and clear distinction, rather than connective tissue, we classified them in “other parameters”.

knowledge_fragments.content: Cutaneous manifestations are frequent and often early features of both Kawasaki disease (KD) and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C). Although these conditions differ in epidemiology and triggers, they share overlapping clinical features and immune-mediated pathogenic mechanisms, making early recognition and differential diagnosis challenging. Dermatologic findings are particularly relevant, as they may represent the first clinical clue and precede severe systemic complications.

knowledge_fragments.content: Age-related variability further complicates diagnosis. Infants younger than 6 months and adolescents often present with incomplete or atypical features, increasing the risk of delayed diagnosis and coronary complications. For example, a 3-month-old infant with minimal initial symptoms developed coronary aneurysms within days despite early intervention, highlighting the aggressive nature of KD in very young children. Conversely, adolescents may present with prolonged fever, mucocutaneous findings, and systemic symptoms that overlap with infectious or autoimmune diseases, often delaying diagnosis.

She had been presented to national and international experts, including a virtual international expert dysmorphology network. Discussions at the Expert Panel meeting included multiple specialists suggesting the possibility of various RNA processing disorders. A literature review by panel members that evening narrowed the search to a condition with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 1 million.. Confirmed diagnosis: Trichohepatoenteric syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Trichohepatoenteric syndrome.

knowledge_fragments.content: MIS-C emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic as a post—SARS-CoV-2 hyperinflammatory syndrome affecting a small proportion of infected children. It is characterized by persistent fever, laboratory evidence of inflammation, and multisystem involvement, frequently including the cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and mucocutaneous systems. Current evidence supports an immune-mediated pathogenesis driven by post-infectious immune dysregulation, molecular mimicry, and exaggerated cytokine responses. Cutaneous findings occur in approximately 70–75% of cases and display wide morphological variability, ranging from morbilliform and scarlatiniform rashes to urticarial and reticulated patterns. This heterogeneity, combined with substantial overlap with KD-related skin findings, further complicates early diagnostic differentiation.

She also experienced mild limitations in physical activity but did not seek immediate medical attention. Her parents are healthy and not related by blood. In 2017, she visited an ophthalmology hospital where fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography showed no abnormalities. She was prescribed oral pyridostigmine (60 mg tid) and prednisone (30 mg qd), but her symptoms did not significantly improve. The prednisone dosage was gradually reduced to 15 mg qd. In 2018, she experienced fatigue and weakness 6 months postpartum. In September 2019, she stopped taking pyridostigmine and prednisone due to a lack of noticeable improvement in her symptoms. In late 2020, she developed left-sided facial hypoesthesia. In 2021, her eye movement restriction worsened, particularly during the 8th month of pregnancy, accompanied by emotional stress, leading to retesting and strabismus.. tree.case_summary:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a routine well-child checkup. He began walking at 20 months of age. He is able to drink from a cup but cannot use silverware. He speaks in 2-word phrases and can stack 4 blocks. He can scribble but is unable to draw a circle. His height is above the 99th percentile, and his weight is at the 15th percentile. Vital signs are normal. On examination, he has bilateral inferior lens dislocation, long slender fingers, a high-arched palate, and hyperelastic skin. When he wraps one hand around the opposite wrist, his thumb and fifth finger overlap. What is the most likely cause of these findings?

Options:
A. Fibrillin 1 deficiency
B. Procollagen peptidase deficiency
C. Type I collagen mutation
D. Deficiency of pyridoxine-dependent enzymes
E. Alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency
F. Mutation in the FGFR3 gene
G. Type V collagen deficiency
H. Lysyl hydroxylase deficiency
I. Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency
J. Cystathionine synthase deficiency

excluded_candidates: Homocystinuria: less likely due to absence of mention of developmental delay or mental retardation
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: possible but less likely due to absence of skin fragility or poor wound healing
